job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior credit analyst at a regional bank in Birmingham. I read small-business loan applications, check the accounts, and write a short summary for the senior lending officer, who decides. I did finance at a university nearby, passed with a middling grade, no internships, and I've been here five months. My parents run a pharmacy about an hour away, and I live with two flatmates, one of them my cousin Chidi. Weekends I play five-a-side football and go home for Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I thought. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy my loan summaries, and it's useful, but it gets numbers wrong, so I check. To friends I'd say, relax, it's a tool like a calculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is stable. A bank is cautious, and a person has to sign off on a loan. The routine bits get a little faster, and the senior officers keep the decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, learn the job properly. I'd keep saving 350 a month, join the bank's study group for the professional credit qualification, and ask the senior officer, Mr Adeyemi, to let me sit in on loan committees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a steady world, and I like steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think about is my parents' pharmacy. Supermarkets and online chains are squeezing it, and my dad doesn't say, but I think it's tight. I've got about ten thousand saved and I'd help if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody to blame, really. Markets move, big chains win, small shops lose. I'd like the government to be fairer on business rates, but I'm not angry.

Ask to sit in on **loan committees**.
feel: **Calm**; it's a steady world, and I like steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we have to adapt, but not panic. At work I'd say the bank should use it carefully, since a bad loan decision from software could cost millions. To friends, I'd say learn it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my first rung is what gets squeezed. Reading accounts and writing the summary is thinking work, and a good model does it in seconds. The bank may hire fewer juniors, and I'm one of the new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself useful in ways the model isn't: meeting business owners, visiting the premises, judging character. I'd use the chatbot more, systematically, to get good at checking its work. And I'd start the credit qualification this year, not next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the path, but a lot of people will be trying to walk it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summaries, no question. I write about eight a week, and I could probably get the model to do most of the draft. My senior officer would notice when I started asking for more difficult files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the bank to say clearly which roles will change, and to pay for the qualification. Also, I'd ask for a rule that a person always signs off on a loan, so we keep humans in the loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle. I'd say, work out how to share the gains: a tax, a fund, a shorter week. I wouldn't say that loudly at the bank, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Two years isn't time to climb the ladder. The thing a bank pays a junior for, reading and summarising, would be done by something cheaper. And lending itself might be handed to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending, stop the five-a-side league fees, and push savings up toward fourteen thousand. I'd talk to my parents to see if the pharmacy could use help, and I'd look at whether a licence in pharmacy support or insurance is safer. And I'd learn the AI tools so I'm the person who can use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be listening to the news every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask my senior officer, honestly, what he sees coming. Then I'd draw up a budget of exactly what I need to live on, which is about 1,400, so I know how long my money lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents it's serious and I'd tell them I have a cushion. I'd leave out that I might need the pharmacy to hire me, since I don't want them thinking I'm failing.

I wouldn't say that loudly at the bank.

fieldNote: Anxious but **organised**: he starts with budgets and exact numbers, and asks his senior officer for honest information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get ready, but short enough that the plan can't wait. I'd say banks should be honest with staff about what's changing, and governments should fund retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautiously okay. Five years gives me time to make myself valuable: client relationships, judgement, a qualification. I'd be twenty-seven. I'd still worry, but I'd have something to point to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: begin the credit qualification, use AI for the first draft of every summary, and ask to move into relationship management. I'd keep saving, put some in a global index fund, and stay in the flat with my cousin Chidi to keep costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The extra three years help, but they don't make it go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd actually try to do my parents' pharmacy books with the tools, to see if I can make it more profitable. It's a real test, and if it works, it's an option for me too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third into an index fund, because I think I can ride out a few bad years. The rest in savings and the qualification. I'd keep a cushion of six months in cash, and tell Chidi the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and sensible people will use it. I'd say start now, save, learn, and don't believe the loudest voices on either side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. By thirty-two I'd hope to be a senior analyst or a relationship manager, maybe with a share of my parents' pharmacy. Ten years is long enough to take a few sensible risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, with more discipline. Finish the qualification in the first two years, build a reputation with business clients, and invest a larger share of savings. If the pharmacy needs money, I'd put some in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one where I can plan my life like a normal person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could buy a flat, maybe even marry. In two years I'd have put all of that on hold, and I'd have lived on a tight budget the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be where a person is needed, deciding on a loan with a business owner across the table. Or running something of my own, like the pharmacy. The numbers part I'd leave to the machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything in my plan, the qualification, the flat, helping my parents, takes years, and that one gives me two. What would help is a firm that's honest, retraining that's paid for and a bit of luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of change. I'm scared of change that gives me no time to be ready.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of change. I'm scared of change that gives me no time to be ready.
portrait: Emeka is 22, a junior credit analyst at a Birmingham regional bank, five months into his first job.
He uses a chatbot now and then, checks its numbers, and learns tools once they're proven.
A centrist, he blames no one, though he worries about his parents' squeezed pharmacy.
With ten thousand saved and plenty of local jobs he's **uneasy** at worst in slower worlds and anxious when time is short.
With more time he plans a qualification, an index fund, a flat and maybe a stake in the pharmacy.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries him most, because his plans each take years.
whatWouldHelp: He wants an **honest employer**, paid retraining and a little luck.
